## Overview

This report uses unsupervised learning techniques to investigate whether Lower Layer Super Output Areas (LSOAs) in Hull and the East Riding of Yorkshire can be grouped according to selected demographic, health and socio-economic characteristics derived from the 2021 Census.

The aim is to identify whether distinct types of neighbourhood emerge naturally from the data without using any predefined labels or outcome variables.

In this section, briefly describe:

- what is being clustered (LSOAs)
- the characteristics used to describe them
- why clustering is an appropriate tool for identifying groups of similar neighbourhoods

You may wish to write a short paragraph similar to:

> This report uses unsupervised learning techniques to investigate whether neighbourhoods in Hull and the East Riding of Yorkshire can be grouped according to patterns of health, disability, economic activity and household characteristics. The objective is to explore whether distinct types of communities emerge naturally from the data.

Do not describe code or implementation details here.

## The data

The data are derived from the 2021 UK Census and were extracted from a number of published census tables.

The analysis combines information from five Census 2021 Topic Summary datasets published by the Office for National Statistics (ONS): General Health (TS037), Disability (TS038), Car or Van Availability (TS045), National Statistics Socio-economic Classification (TS062) and Economic Activity Status (TS066). These tables were linked using the LSOA geography code to create a single analysis dataset.

- TS037 [General health of usual residents](https://www.ons.gov.uk/datasets/TS037)
- TS038 [Disability status](https://www.ons.gov.uk/datasets/TS038)
- TS045 [Household car or van availability](https://www.ons.gov.uk/datasets/TS045)
- TS062 [National Statistics Socio-economic Classification (NS-SEC)](https://www.ons.gov.uk/datasets/TS062)
- TS066 [Economic activity status (usual residents aged 16+)](https://www.ons.gov.uk/datasets/TS066)





The analysis focuses on LSOAs located within:

- Kingston upon Hull
- East Riding of Yorkshire

Each row in the analysis dataset corresponds to a single LSOA.

### Combining Census tables

The dataset was created by joining information from several Census 2021 tables using the LSOA geography code.

The source tables include information on:

- self-reported health
- disability status
- vehicle availability
- socio-economic classification
- economic activity

The resulting dataset combines measures describing different aspects of neighbourhood composition within a single table suitable for analysis.

### Variables supplied for analysis

The coursework pipeline initially selects the following variables:

- `n_unhealthy`
- `n_healthy`
- `n_disabled`
- `n_no_cars`
- `n_unskilled`
- `n_unestablished`
- `n_long_term_sick`

These variables represent counts of residents within each LSOA falling into particular Census categories.

### Variable definitions

The supplied variables are derived from Census categories as follows:

- `n_unhealthy` – residents reporting bad or very bad health
- `n_healthy` – residents reporting good or very good health
- `n_disabled` – residents reporting a disability
- `n_no_cars` – households with no access to a car or van
- `n_unskilled` – residents in lower supervisory, semi-routine or routine occupations
- `n_unestablished` – residents who are students, never worked, or long-term unemployed
- `n_long_term_sick` – economically inactive residents who report being long-term sick or disabled

### Important

The default analysis uses these count variables because they are selected in:

`scripts/unsupervised/01_load_data_cw.py`

However, the SQL query used to create the dataset also calculates several proportion variables.

For example:

- proportion unhealthy
- proportion disabled
- proportion with no vehicle access
- proportion long-term sick

You are encouraged to consider whether clustering on counts or proportions gives a more meaningful representation of neighbourhood similarity.

Modifying the variable selection is part of the analytical task.

If you choose to experiment with alternative variables, commit your changes regularly to GitHub and explain your decisions in the report.

## Interpretation of the variables

Before clustering, think carefully about what these variables represent.

The supplied variables are counts rather than proportions. As a result:

- larger LSOAs may tend to have larger values for many variables
- some apparent differences may reflect population size rather than social characteristics
- highly populated areas may appear similar simply because many counts are large

This means that clusters based on counts may partly reflect neighbourhood size.

Proportion variables may reduce this effect by describing the composition of an area rather than the total number of residents.

You may discuss and explore these issues within your analysis.

## Hierarchical clustering

Hierarchical clustering identifies groups of similar LSOAs without requiring the number of clusters to be specified in advance.

You should:

- state the distance metric used
- state the linkage method used
- briefly justify your choices
- explain what the dendrogram represents

## Visualising clusters using PCA

Principal Components Analysis (PCA) can be used to visualise high-dimensional data in two dimensions.

You should explain:

- what PCA does in general terms
- why PCA is useful for visualising clustering results
- whether the clusters appear well separated

![PCA, first two dimensions with cluster membership](../../artefacts/unsupervised/cw/hcluster_scatter.jpg)

Remember that PCA is a visualisation tool and does not determine the clusters itself.

## K-Means clustering

K-Means clustering requires the number of clusters to be specified in advance.

You should:

- interpret the resulting clusters

## Comparison and interpretation

Compare the hierarchical clustering and K-Means results.

You may consider:

- whether both methods produce similar groupings
- whether certain LSOAs consistently belong together
- which clustering appears easier to interpret
- whether differences between methods change your conclusions

Remember that clustering is exploratory. Careful interpretation and justification are more important than finding a single "correct" answer.

## Limitations and extensions

Discuss limitations of your analysis.

Possible limitations include:

- use of a limited number of Census variables
- sensitivity to scaling choices
- use of counts rather than proportions
- population size influencing the results
- difficulty assigning real-world meaning to some clusters

Possible extensions include:

- using proportion variables instead of counts
- including additional Census variables
- applying alternative clustering methods
- exploring clusters geographically
- comparing Hull and East Riding separately

You do not need to implement all of these extensions to achieve a high mark. However, you should demonstrate an ability to modify and extend the analysis pipeline where appropriate.

## Conclusion

Summarise your findings in three or four sentences.

You should briefly state:

- what patterns were identified
- whether meaningful groups of neighbourhoods emerged
- what remained uncertain
- what additional work might improve understanding of the data

Do not introduce new results in the conclusion.
